title: Europe's next-wave AI data centers sit 175 km from major hubs — up from 46 km
subtitle: DC Byte tracks nine planned gigawatt-plus European sites; only one is near a major city as developers chase cheaper power in rural Spain and northern Sweden.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Data-center intelligence firm DC Byte published figures this week showing European AI data centers planned for 2026–2028 will sit an average of 175 kilometers from major metro hubs, up from 46 kilometers for sites delivered between 2022 and 2025. Powered-land in the traditional FLAP-D cluster (Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, Dublin) runs about €2.36 million per megawatt; in tertiary cities the cost drops to roughly €512,000 per megawatt. Of the nine gigawatt-plus European projects DC Byte is tracking, only one — near Paris — sits close to a major hub.

The reason is grid queue, not preference. Training runs for frontier models draw hundreds of megawatts sustained, and the transmission operators around the FLAP-D metros are quoting multi-year interconnect timelines. Rural Spain and northern Sweden are attractive because they have unused renewable capacity, faster planning permission, and, in Sweden's case, cold climates that cut cooling loads. Greenfield sites now make up 39% of Europe's future data-center pipeline versus just 8% of already-delivered projects — the fastest structural shift the sector has seen since the FLAP-D consensus formed a decade ago.

The pattern reshapes several downstream questions. Latency to end users goes up, so inference workloads still cluster near cities while training moves out. National governments now compete more openly on grid connections, tax treatment, and sovereignty rules — Spain's Aragon region and Sweden's Boden corridor have already signed multi-gigawatt letters of intent. And workforce and community-impact politics that had been contained to a few hubs are now being exported to towns that never expected to host a 500-megawatt load.

For learners: the map of where AI happens is moving under your feet. When you read that a frontier model was trained on 100,000 GPUs, ask where those GPUs actually sit — increasingly, in a Spanish or Swedish field connected to a hydroelectric or wind grid, not in a Frankfurt suburb. Infrastructure geography is becoming as important to AI as model architecture, and the next five years of policy fights will be about who gets the interconnect.
